entityDossier.whatItIs: Lockheed Martin Advanced Development Programs, universally known as Skunk Works: the unacknowledged-program aeronautics organisation founded by Clarence 'Kelly' Johnson in 1943 at Burbank, California, and now resident at Air Force Plant 42, Palmdale, a government-owned contractor-operated facility. Ben Rich directed it from 1975 to 1991. Its programme list is the working definition of the black aircraft: the U-2, the A-12 and SR-71, the F-117, Sea Shadow, DarkStar and the RQ-170 Sentinel.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: Skunk Works is the operational proof of the board's central structural claim: that a private corporation can hold, fly and conceal hardware from everyone without a need to know, including senior officers in the chain of command, for years at a time. AARO's own Historical Record Report uses Skunk Works aircraft to explain a class of UAP reports, and in doing so concedes the point -- the organisation routinely fields flying objects whose existence the government denies while they are flying. As of the 1986 GAO pass it also carries a documented custody failure: the companion report to GAO's testimony of 24 July 1986 names the Lockheed/Burbank plant as the site where special-access document control deteriorated, and says the deterioration might not have happened had the Defense Investigative Service been permitted to inspect the contract as it inspected Lockheed's others.
entityDossier.narrative:
The reason Skunk Works belongs at programme level on this board is not that anyone has documented anomalous material inside it. It is that Skunk Works settles an argument the board otherwise has to make by inference. The standing objection to every legacy-programme account is that a secret of this size could not be kept -- too many people, too many decades, too many contractors. Skunk Works is the counter-example the United States government publishes about itself: the RQ-170 flew operationally for years before Lockheed acknowledged it existed, and the acknowledgment came after a loss on foreign soil rather than on a schedule anyone chose. The concealment worked until physics interrupted it.

What the 1986 GAO material adds is the failure mode. Concealment of that quality is not free, and the price is paid in accountability: 1,460 discrepancies in a 40,000-item special-access inventory at one company, 11 still unresolved, discovered because a congressional subcommittee asked rather than because the security system surfaced it. GAO's own explanation of why nobody caught it earlier is the sentence this board keeps returning to -- special access contracts are 'carved out of the Defense Investigative Service's periodic inspection program', by a 1965 decision, and by 1983 there were probably several thousand of them.

The organisation therefore sits on this board twice over: as the demonstration that unacknowledged hardware can be held indefinitely, and as the documented case where holding it meant nobody could say where the paper went.

claims.text: Lockheed Martin's Advanced Development Programs organisation developed the RQ-170 Sentinel and the DarkStar, and AARO cites Skunk Works aircraft as the explanation for a class of UAP reports.
claims.source: AARO, Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena, Volume I

claims.text: Ben Rich directed the organisation from 1975 to 1991 and published a memoir describing its compartmentation, security and funding practice.
claims.source: Ben R. Rich and Leo Janos, Skunk Works: A Personal Memoir of My Years at Lockheed

claims.text: GAO/NSIAD-86-191 of 7 August 1986 names 'the Lockheed/Burbank plant' as the location of the special access contract whose document accountability deteriorated, and states the deterioration 'may not have occurred if the Defense Investigative Service had been permitted to conduct semiannual inspections of the contract, as it does with other contracts at Lockheed.'
claims.source: GAO/NSIAD-86-191, Information Security: Need for DOD Inspections of Special Access Contracts, B-223830, 7 August 1986, https://www.gao.gov/assets/nsiad-86-191.pdf

claims.text: The testimony that preceded that report declined to identify the programme or the service involved: 'As part of DOD granting us access to the special access program to respond your request, we agreed not to identify the nature of the program or the specific DOD component or military service involved.'
claims.source: GAO accession 130581, statement of Martin M. Ferber, 24 July 1986, footnote, https://www.gao.gov/assets/130581.pdf

entityDossier.denialPosture: Skunk Works does not deny; it declines to confirm, and the record shows the decline holding for years at a time and then ending on someone else's timetable. The RQ-170 is the canonical instance: operational, photographed, and unacknowledged until it was lost abroad. The 1986 GAO exchange is the same posture at the paperwork layer -- GAO was granted access on condition that it not name the programme, the component or the service, so the public record of the failure exists with the subject of the failure redacted out of it. The board treats that as a documented behaviour rather than an inference, because in both cases the concealment and its terms are described in a government document.
connections: Named as the Lockheed/Burbank plant in GAO/NSIAD-86-191, the companion report to the 1986 testimony carried here as gao-130581.
A division of lockheed-martin, the contractor whose special-access document control the 1986 testimony examined.
Cited by aaro-historical-record-vol1 as the explanation for a class of UAP reports.
openQuestions: GAO/NSIAD-88-2BR, 'Information Security: Actions Taken To Improve Lockheed's Special Access Document Accountability', is the follow-up that would say whether anything changed after 1986. It appeared in a search result only and has not been opened; nothing on this board is cited to it.

The 1986 testimony and its companion report never name the special access programme itself, by agreement with DoD. Whether that programme has since been acknowledged, and under what name, is not established from any document read here.

Ben Rich's post-retirement remarks about technologies 'locked up in black projects' remain the most quoted and least documented artefact in this field. No primary recording or contemporaneous transcript has been located, and the board carries no Tier 1 or Tier 2 claim resting on them.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The United States Air Force, established as an independent military department on 18 September 1947, eleven weeks after the Roswell press release issued by the 509th Bomb Group at Roswell Army Air Field. It inherited and ran every official American UFO project -- Project SIGN in 1948, Project GRUDGE in 1949 and Project BLUE BOOK from 1952 to 1969 -- at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, the installation every retrieval account since 1947 names as the destination of recovered material.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The Air Force is the origin point of both the American UFO record and the American denial record, and it is the only institution on this board that is simultaneously the collector, the analyst, the custodian and the public voice. Under AFR 200-2 it required reports to flow to the Air Technical Intelligence Center -- the foreign-materiel exploitation shop -- and restricted public discussion to cases conclusively identified as conventional. It closed Blue Book publicly in December 1969 while its own units continued to run a Foreign Materiel Program whose 1967 unit history lists MOON DUST and BLUE FLY alongside MIG-17 exploitation and describes airlifting recovered materiel to Wright-Patterson. And in February 1985 an Air Force spokesman, reminded that his own department had published Aurora's figures in an unclassified procurement document, said his orders were still to say only that it was a classified program.
entityDossier.narrative:
Everything this board argues about custody runs through one service, and the useful thing a dossier can do is set the public record and the internal record side by side using only documents.

The public record is well known and well sourced. From 1947 to 1969, 12,618 sightings were reported to Project BLUE BOOK, of which 701 remain unidentified; on 17 December 1969 the Secretary of the Air Force announced its termination, resting on the University of Colorado study and a National Academy of Sciences review; the files went to the National Archives as 94 rolls of microfilm, T-1206. Two later reports attributed the Roswell debris to Project MOGUL and the bodies to anthropomorphic test dummies dropped in the 1950s -- an explanation requiring witnesses to have misdated events by up to a decade.

The internal record is the same service, described by its own units. AFR 200-2 of 26 August 1953, signed by order of the Secretary of the Air Force by Nathan Twining, designated ATIC as the analysis authority, directed that 'All evidence will be forwarded to ATIC', instructed units to safeguard materiel against 'defacing or alteration which would reduce its value for technical analysis', and limited public release to objects 'conclusively identified by ATIC as a conventional aerial device'. Fourteen years later, and two years before Blue Book closed, the 1127th USAF Field Activities Group's own semiannual history lists Project BLUE FLY and Project MOON DUST under FOREIGN MATERIEL PROGRAM, records exploitation personnel deployed to crash sites, and describes about three tons of parts airlifted to Wright-Patterson under a Joint Chiefs priority designation. JANAP 146 was still listing unidentified flying objects as a reportable category in 1977.

None of that establishes anomalous material. All of it establishes that the collection channel the public was told had closed was not the only channel, and that the service said so in documents it classified rather than published.

claims.text: From 1947 to 1969 a total of 12,618 sightings were reported to Project BLUE BOOK, of which 701 remain 'Unidentified'.
claims.source: National Archives, Project BLUE BOOK record group description

claims.text: On 17 December 1969 the Secretary of the Air Force announced the termination of Project BLUE BOOK, relying on the University of Colorado's 'Scientific Study of Unidentified Flying Objects' and a National Academy of Sciences review of it.
claims.source: National Archives, Project BLUE BOOK record group description

claims.text: AFR 200-2 of 26 August 1953, signed by order of the Secretary of the Air Force by N. F. Twining, designated ATIC as the analysis authority, directed that 'All evidence will be forwarded to ATIC', and limited releasable information to the fact that an object had been 'conclusively identified by ATIC as a conventional aerial device or other familiar object'.

The 1127th USAF Field Activities Group's own semiannual history for 1 January to 30 June 1967 lists Project BLUE FLY, MIG-17 Exploitation and Project MOON DUST together under FOREIGN MATERIEL PROGRAM, and records that the unit 'coordinated requirements necessary to deploy the FTD exploitation personnel and to airlift personnel and parts from site of acquisition to Wright-Patterson AFB. The take consisted of approximately three tons of aircraft parts and armament.'
claims.source: History, 1127 USAF Field Activities Group (AFNIA), 1 January - 30 June 1967, doc. AFNIABA 014-67, pp. 29-30, https://nsarchive2.gwu.edu/NSAEBB/NSAEBB520-the-Pentagons-Spies/EBB-PS03a.pdf

claims.text: Reminded in February 1985 that the Pentagon's own unclassified P-1 procurement document had put Aurora's funding in the public domain, 'an Air Force spokesman said his orders still were to say only: It's a classified program.'

entityDossier.denialPosture: The Air Force's posture is not silence but re-description, and it is the same shape in 1953, 1969 and 1985. In 1953 the regulation permitted public discussion of identified objects and forbade it for unidentified ones, which converts every open case into a non-statement. In 1969 the public collection channel was closed with a scientific justification while the foreign-materiel channel continued under separate authority. In 1985 the service declined to confirm a programme whose figures its own department had already published, on standing orders. In each case the denial is procedural rather than substantive: not 'this did not happen' but 'this is not a thing I am permitted to describe' -- which is why the board grades the Aurora edge as a directed denial with the Air Force named as its issuer, and why nothing here is graded as a denial of anomalous material, which the service has not been documented making in these records.
connections: Parent service of usaf-1127th-field-activities-group, whose 1967 history documents the MOON DUST and BLUE FLY recovery pipeline terminating at Wright-Patterson.
Issued afr-200-2, which routed all evidence to atic and restricted public release to identified objects.
Named as the denier on the aurora-budget-line edge: the spokesman who called the programme classified after the Pentagon published its figures.
openQuestions: The 1127th USAF Field Activities Group's activation and inactivation dates are not established. No primary lineage record was found, and its Fort Belvoir station appears only in secondary accounts.
The US deorbit figure on page 30 of the 1127th's 1 January - 30 June 1967 history is illegible in the released scan at 340 dpi and is not reported anywhere on this board.

The FY1986 Department of Defense Procurement Programs (P-1) exhibit that carried the Aurora line has not been located or read. Everything on this board about its contents comes from a named Washington Post correspondent reporting them in February 1985.
ATIC's 1947-1951 T-2 intelligence files have never been subject to a comprehensive declassification review.
